lessons.title: Why Volatility Reverts Even When Prices Don't

children.text: Chapter 1 used the March 2020 Covid-19 crash to show that the Nifty 50's price eventually reverted, climbing to fresh highs within about ten months, while a random walk with drift has no fixed price level to return to in the first place. There is a second, sharper story hiding in that same month. The Nifty's price never actually went back to where it was before the crash, it kept moving forward along a completely new path. Its volatility, on the other hand, genuinely did come back. Within months, the wild, panicked, multi-percent daily swings of March 2020 calmed back down to something close to the market's normal, pre-crisis temperament. Same event, same index, two completely different kinds of reversion.

body.text: A price series can wander forever with no fixed home, exactly the random walk from Lesson 3. Its volatility, the amplitude of its day-to-day wiggles, behaves completely differently. Volatility is driven by things that are inherently self-limiting: uncertainty resolves, panic exhausts itself, forced selling ends. That is why volatility reliably reverts to a long-run normal level even for a stock or index whose price itself never comes back to where it started.

children.text: Realized Volatility: Measuring the Wiggle, Not the Direction

markDefs.definition: The forward-looking volatility implied by current options prices, as opposed to realized volatility, which is backward-looking and calculated from historical price data. India VIX, covered fully in Lesson 14, is an implied volatility measure.

children.text: Realized volatility measures how much a price has actually been moving, regardless of direction, calculated as the standard deviation of daily returns, usually scaled up to an annualized figure by multiplying by the square root of 252, the approximate number of trading days in a year. This is different from

, which looks forward instead of backward. This lesson works with realized volatility, since it is the more direct, mechanical measure to build reversion intuition on before Lesson 14 introduces India VIX.

body.caption: Annualizing a daily standard deviation of returns into the conventional annualized volatility figure quoted across Indian and global markets.

children.text: A stock whose daily returns have a standard deviation of 1.2% has an annualized realized volatility of 1.2% times the square root of 252, which is roughly 19.0%. That single number is the stock's typical, day-to-day "temperature". A calm, large-cap FMCG name might run at 15 to 20%. A volatile, news-driven smallcap might run at 45% or higher. Both numbers tend to have their own long-run normal level that they keep drifting back toward, however different those normal levels are from each other.
Why Volatility Is More Reliably Mean-Reverting Than Price

A price is anchored to permanent, fundamental information. If a company's earning power genuinely and permanently improves or deteriorates, the market is correct to send the price to a new level and never look back, exactly the structural growth and structural decline cases from Lesson 3. Volatility is not anchored to fundamentals the same way. It is driven by uncertainty, and uncertainty is inherently temporary: an earnings date passes and the outcome becomes known, a policy announcement is made and the ambiguity resolves, a wave of forced selling from margin calls or a fund's redemptions runs its course and stops. None of these forces have a reason to keep pushing volatility higher forever, because their entire cause is the passage of time resolving a temporary unknown. This is a big part of why volatility is, in practice, one of the more reliably mean-reverting quantities in finance, more so than most individual stock prices.

body.title: Nifty 50: price path vs realized volatility around March 2020 (illustrative)

body.text: Follow both lines to month 12. The price line does not return to 100, it moves on and settles above its pre-crash level, following a completely new trajectory that has nothing to do with retracing the crash. The volatility line does return, close to its pre-crash reading of around 16%. This is the whole lesson in one chart: price found a new home. Volatility found its old one.

children.text: The Apparent Paradox: Clustering vs Reversion

markDefs.definition: The well-documented tendency for large price moves to be followed by more large moves, and calm days to be followed by more calm days, regardless of direction. First formalized in Robert Engle's ARCH and GARCH models.

children.text: If negative autocorrelation is the signature of mean reversion, as Lesson 6 established, a sharp reader should be suspicious here. Volatility is famous for

, a high-volatility day tends to be followed by another high-volatility day, which sounds like positive autocorrelation, the fingerprint of momentum, not reversion. Both things are true at once, because they operate at different time horizons. Clustering describes short-term persistence: tomorrow's volatility is well predicted by today's, over a horizon of days. Mean reversion describes what happens over a longer horizon: weeks to months out, that same volatility drifts back down toward its long-run average, however elevated it is right now. GARCH-family models, the industry-standard way to forecast volatility, are built on exactly this combination, a persistent, sticky short-term component layered on top of a longer-run pull back toward a stable average, both features living in the same model without contradicting each other.

body.title: Annualize a stock's realized volatility
body.prompt: A stock's daily returns have a standard deviation of 1.5%. What is its annualized realized volatility, rounded to one decimal place, in percent?
body.explanation: 1.5% x sqrt(252) = 1.5% x 15.87 = 23.8%. This is a moderately volatile stock, well above a calm large-cap's typical 15 to 20% range.

body.title: Clustering and reversion, reconciled
body.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between volatility clustering and volatility mean reversion?
options: They contradict each other. If volatility mean-reverts, it cannot also cluster
They describe different time horizons: clustering is short-term day-to-day persistence, mean reversion is the longer-run pull back toward a stable average
Clustering is simply another name for mean reversion
Only one of the two is actually observed in real markets
body.explanation: Clustering and mean reversion coexist because they operate at different horizons. Day to day, high volatility tends to be followed by more high volatility, clustering. Over weeks to months, that elevated volatility still drifts back down toward its long-run average, reversion. GARCH-family models are built to capture both effects in a single framework.

cards.definition: A backward-looking measure of how much a price has actually moved, calculated as the standard deviation of returns over a historical window, commonly annualized by multiplying by the square root of 252.

A forward-looking volatility measure derived from current options prices, reflecting the market's expectation of future price movement. India VIX, covered in Lesson 14, is an implied volatility index.

The tendency for large price moves to be followed by more large moves, and calm periods to be followed by more calm periods, a short-term persistence effect that coexists with longer-run mean reversion.
A family of statistical models, building on Robert Engle's ARCH model, that forecasts volatility by combining short-term persistence (clustering) with reversion toward a long-run average level.

points: Volatility reliably reverts to a long-run normal level for reasons different from price reversion: it is driven by uncertainty, and uncertainty is inherently temporary, resolving as events pass and information becomes known.
Realized volatility measures how much a price has actually moved, typically as an annualized standard deviation of returns. Implied volatility, covered next, looks forward instead of backward.

A price can settle onto a completely new, permanent trajectory after a crash without ever returning to its old level, while its volatility genuinely does return to something close to its old normal, the same March 2020 episode viewed through two different lenses.

Volatility clustering (short-term persistence) and volatility mean reversion (a longer-run pull back to average) are not contradictory. They operate at different time horizons and are both built into standard GARCH-family volatility models.

Because volatility's mean-reverting behavior is unusually reliable compared to price, it is a natural next domain for a systematic reversion strategy, which Lesson 14 builds using India's own volatility benchmark.
